Verba
Latin dictionary and practice — look up any word, even when the ending has changed

Type the word exactly as it appears in your reading. You don’t need to know the dictionary form first — that’s what this is for. Macrons are fine, and j/v or i/u both work.

Type an English word and you’ll get the Latin words that can mean it. Simple, common words work best — try carry rather than transporting.

Try:

Every result has three parts

  1. The dictionary form in red — how the word is listed in a dictionary. For amaverunt that’s amo, amare, amavi, amatus. This is what you write in a vocab list.
  2. What it means — love, like.
  3. What your form is doing — perfect active indicative 3rd person plural. The grey line underneath says what that means in ordinary English: who is doing it, and when. Here, “they” are doing it and it already happened — so, “they loved.”

If a word shows several forms, Latin spelled them the same way and only the sentence tells you which one is meant. Read the plain-English notes and pick the one that fits.

Make a vocab list

Type or paste one Latin word per line. The meanings and principal parts fill in automatically from the dictionary, so a bare list of words is enough. To write your own meaning instead, use porto = to carry.

    Practice it

    Why the practice works this way — worth two minutes
    • Recall before you look. Trying to remember, and failing, teaches more than re-reading the answer. That’s why the card asks you to say it out loud first.
    • Spread out over days. Words you get right come back later and later; words you miss come back soon. Cramming feels better and works worse.
    • Missed words return on a steady gap — about five cards later — rather than at the end of the round. Even spacing beats stretching the gap for what you still remember next week.
    • Mixed practice. Jumbling meanings, endings, and word types is harder in the moment and stronger later than drilling one thing at a time.
    • Common words first. Around a thousand core words make up roughly 78% of Caesar and 70% of the Aeneid, so they repay study far more than rare ones.
    • Say what it reminds you of. The back of each card shows the Latin stem and asks what English words come from it — making the link yourself is what fixes it.

    Based on research on retrieval practice (Roediger & Karpicke), spacing (Cepeda et al.), interval schedules (Karpicke & Roediger 2007), interleaving (Rohrer & Taylor), and core-vocabulary coverage (Dickinson College Commentaries). Latin reading fluency still comes mostly from reading a lot of Latin — this is for the vocabulary and forms that make the reading possible.

    Try to answer before you check — the attempt itself is what builds the memory, and getting it wrong does no harm here. Every word you miss is rescheduled to come back sooner; every word you know is pushed further out.
